results.authors: Montalban X, Lebrun-Frenay C, Oh J, et al.
results.key_findings: Five regions for dissemination in space (periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, optic nerve); kFLC index accepted as an alternative to CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands; central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting MRI markers; additional supporting evidence recommended in people over 50 or with vascular risk factors.
results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2024 revisions of the McDonald criteria

results.authors: Wattjes MP, Ciccarelli O, Reich DS, et al.
results.key_findings: Consensus MRI protocol for suspected MS: brain MRI with 3D FLAIR, T2, DWI and pre- and post-gadolinium T1, and spinal cord MRI at diagnosis; gadolinium at baseline to show active lesions.
results.title: 2021 MAGNIMS-CMSC-NAIMS consensus recommendations on the use of MRI in patients with multiple sclerosis

results.authors: Wingerchuk DM, Banwell B, Bennett JL, et al.
results.key_findings: NMOSD with AQP4-IgG requires one core clinical characteristic (optic neuritis, acute myelitis, area postrema syndrome, acute brainstem, diencephalic or cerebral syndrome) and a positive cell-based AQP4-IgG assay; seronegative NMOSD requires additional clinical and MRI criteria.
results.title: International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders

output.summary: The 2024 revision of the McDonald criteria (Montalban et al., Lancet Neurol 2025) adds the optic nerve as a fifth region, accepts the kFLC index as an alternative to oligoclonal bands, and allows the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions as supporting markers. Lesions in four or five regions establish dissemination in space without a separate test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, positive CSF or the central vein sign is needed. In people over 50 or with vascular risk factors, additional supporting evidence is recommended.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not attribute the earlier bilateral leg numbness to lumbar radiculopathy: it was a sensory myelitis and counts as a prior attack
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria: two attacks (sensory myelitis 8 months ago, current right optic neuritis) with DIS in all five regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord, right optic nerve on MRI and VEP) and enhancing and non-enhancing lesions

Treat the optic neuritis (acuity 20/70 with a RAPD) with methylprednisolone IV 1 g daily for 3 days or oral 500 mg daily for 5 days, after a urine dipstick excludes infection (she has urinary frequency); explain that steroids speed recovery but do not change the final visual outcome
Assess the urinary frequency with a post-void residual: an antimuscarinic if the residual is low, intermittent self-catheterisation if it is raised
Explain that heat-triggered transient worsening (Uhthoff phenomenon) is not a new relapse, and advise cooling

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (two attacks in 8 months, enhancing optic nerve and brain lesions, residual paraparesis), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception
Before an anti-CD20 or S1P modulator, check HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV antibody and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive) and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Denise Carter is a 37-year-old right-handed African American woman who presents to the emergency department with a 4-day history of progressive visual loss in her right eye accompanied by a deep, aching retro-orbital pain that worsens with eye movements, particularly lateral gaze and upward gaze. She initially noticed mild blurring of her right visual field while grading papers four evenings ago, which she attributed to eye strain after prolonged screen use. Over the subsequent 48 hours, the blurring progressed substantially, and she began to notice that colors, especially reds and greens, appeared faded or washed out when she covered her left eye and looked solely through the right. The retro-orbital pain developed on the second day and has been constant, rated at 5 out of 10 in intensity, worsened by eye movement but not by bright light. By the morning of presentation, she described her right eye vision as looking through a frosted window, which prompted her husband to bring her to the emergency department. On further questioning, she reports that approximately eight months ago she experienced a prolonged episode of numbness and tingling affecting both lower extremities from the mid-thigh downward, which developed over two to three days and persisted for roughly four weeks before gradually resolving. She visited an urgent care clinic at that time and was told it was likely a pinched nerve in her back, but no imaging studies were obtained. She notes that she still occasionally experiences brief tingling in her feet, particularly in the evenings or when she is fatigued. She also describes that over the past months the tingling in her feet and a heaviness in her legs become noticeably worse when she takes hot showers or after vigorous exercise, returning to baseline after cooling down. Over the past several months, she reports progressive fatigue that is disproportionate to her activity level, difficulty concentrating during afternoon classes, and an episode approximately three months ago where her right leg felt unusually heavy and stiff while walking up stairs, which resolved after resting for several minutes. She denies any fevers, unintentional weight loss, joint pain, skin rashes, oral ulcers, dry eyes, or dry mouth. She denies any history of seizures, difficulty swallowing, or bowel or bladder incontinence, although she notes increased urinary frequency over the past two months that she had attributed to drinking more coffee.
